paragraphs.heading: Engineering with quantum rules
paragraphs.text: Quantum engineering is the development of technology that takes advantage of the laws of quantum mechanics. It uses those laws to build things such as quantum sensors and quantum computers. It is growing into an engineering discipline of its own. There is a bachelor of quantum engineering at the University of New South Wales, and the Universität des Saarlandes offers both a Bachelor and a Master of Science in it.

paragraphs.heading: Who is paying for it
paragraphs.text: Since 2010, several governments have created programmes for quantum technologies; one is the UK National Quantum Technologies Programme. In 2016 the European Union launched the Quantum Technology Flagship, a €1 Billion project running 10 years. The United States passed its National Quantum Initiative Act in December 2018, which gives quantum research a US$1 billion budget each year. China is putting up what will be the largest quantum research facility in the world, with 76 billion Yuan planned for it, and large companies have invested as well.

paragraphs.heading: Secure communication
paragraphs.text: Quantum secure communication is thought to stay safe even once quantum computers can run Shor's algorithm to break current cryptography. One technique, quantum key distribution (QKD), sends information using entangled light so that any interception is obvious to the user. A quantum random number generator produces truly random numbers, unlike ordinary algorithms that only imitate randomness. Also, a qubit cannot be copied, because measuring a quantum system changes it.

paragraphs.heading: Computers and simulators
paragraphs.text: Quantum computing replaces the classical bit with the qubit, a two-level quantum system that can be 1, 0, or any superposition of the two. Quantum computers are famous mainly because they are expected to be able to run Shor's algorithm, a method that can factor large numbers. Quantum simulators are quantum computers meant to imitate a real system, such as a chemical compound, an idea Richard Feynman first published in 1982. They are simpler to build than general-purpose quantum computers because they do not need complete control over every component.

paragraphs.heading: Very precise sensing
paragraphs.text: Quantum sensing uses certain quantum features to make very precise measurements. Neutral atoms and trapped ions are used as sensors because they are fairly easy to manipulate and to put into a well-known state. Hoped-for uses include positioning systems, communication technology, electric and magnetic field sensors, and gravimetry. In civil engineering, measurements from quantum gravimetry may help reveal unknown conditions underground.

paragraphs.heading: Sensors in medicine
paragraphs.text: Quantum sensors are also being considered in medicine. They could pick up the conductivity of arteries and organs, the firing of neurons, how chemotherapy is progressing, and isotopes inside the body. Methods include spin entanglement, atomic spins used as magnetic sensors, and squeezed light. The results could help diagnose heart problems, malnutrition, early-stage osteoporosis, kidney disease and certain cancers.
